newsitem.title: FINLAND: U.S. holds to NATO stance as Clinton lands.
newsitem.headline: U.S. holds to NATO stance as Clinton lands.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton arrived in Helsinki on Thursday for a summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin, with U.S. officials accompanying him insisting NATO's planned eastward expansion will go ahead.

Clinton, who is recovering from knee surgery, was taken off his Air Force One aircraft in a wheelchair at Helsinki's Vantaa airport. He waved and smiled but made no remarks ahead of the summit, which begins with a dinner on Thursday evening.

The meeting, the first between the two leaders in nearly a year, is expected to concentrate on three areas: the planned expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), arms control and Russian economic reform.

U.S. officials have been adamant that the expansion will go forward despite bitter objections by Russia, which feels that adding neighbouring countries to the 16-member security alliance will isolate and threaten it.
U.S. officials told reporters travelling with Clinton that they did not expect Russia to change its position on the matter, but that an amicable outcome was possible.

"We're going to disagree on NATO enlargement and I don't expect them to change their views and they shouldn't expect us to change our views," National Security Adviser Sandy Berger told reporters. "But on this issue, we will agree to disagree."
The NATO plan is to invite new members -- probably Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- to join the security alliance at a summit scheduled to be held in Madrid in July.

"I think they have to understand that we have a schedule that is going to go forward and that is the track that we are going to pursue," Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told reporters on Air Force One.

Albright said the United States attached great importance to NATO negotiating a separate charter with Russia to chart their future relations, saying Russia must understand that NATO does not pose a threat to it.

"I think they are looking at what they see as the old NATO," Albright said. "They have not yet internalised what it is that we have been telling them .... that this is not a NATO that is structured to defend against them."
On Wednesday, Russia launched a fierce attack on NATO expansion, saying it would be the West's biggest blunder since the end of the Cold War.

"The very discussion of NATO expansion eastwards has already cast a shadow to a certain extent over relations between the West and Russia, the U.S. and Russia," Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told reporters in Helsinki.
"I think ... that we have been robbed to a certain extent of the most valuable achievement of the period since the Cold War -- trust," he added.
Albright said she did not think that trust had eroded, adding that the West was not seeking to undermine Russia.
"I think a point they have misunderstood ... is that we aren't looking for a weak Russia, we're looking for a strong Russia," she told reporters.
Berger concurred: "We will continue ... to try to convey to them that this is not directed at them, just as we need to convey to the American people that Russia is changing," he added.
